newsitem.title: FRANCE: French police swoop on Moslems after bombing.
newsitem.headline: French police swoop on Moslems after bombing.

text.p: French police rounded up a dozen suspected Moslem militants in dawn raids across Paris on Tuesday, a week after a bomb ripped through a city train and killed four people, police said.

Police and counter-espionage officers searched buildings housing Moslems in the capital and the suburbs on orders from anti-terrorism magistrates investigating the attack at Port-Royal station last Tuesday.
Police said that a dozen people had been detained for questioning.

Searches were carried out in the Essone department south of Paris, where a 13 kg (28lb) gas canister similar to that used in the train bombing was detonated in Saint-Maurice Grandcouronne on the night of November 19, shattering a roadman's shed in what may have been a test of the device.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe met Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre on Tuesday morning, but Debre refused to comment on the raids or on his talks with Juppe.

No one has claimed responsibility for the rush-hour train bombing, which killed four people and injured 94. It bore similarities to a 1995 wave of bombings by Algerian Moslem extremists that killed eight people and injured more than 160.
Last year's bombing wave ended after dozens of suspects were rounded up in raids around France.

Roland Jacquard, head of the International Observatory of Terrorism, said Tuesday's raids seemed partly aimed at tracking down people with links to Ali Touchent, one of the main Algerian suspects in last year's bombings who is still free.

"This operation targets Moslem fundamentalists who had been in and out of Belgium and northern France, and who belonged to networks run by Ahmed Zaoui, the (former) chief of Algeria's Islamic Armed Group (GIA) who had (previously) been arrested," Jacquard told France Info radio.
He said such raids were not necessarily to catch the bombers. The aim was to seize clues such as address books and arms and to disorganise networks.

Last year the investigators' main break came when one of the guerrillas, Khaled Kelkal, was identified from a fingerprint on a bomb that failed to explode by a railway track near the central city of Lyon.
His address book in turn led to identification of suspected accomplices who are now in detention. Kelkal was shot dead in a gun battle with police.

Thirty-four Moslem fundamentalists are standing trial in Paris on charges of backing Moroccan guerrillas. Tight security blanketed the trial as it opened on Monday amid fears that last week's bomb was timed to protest at the trial.
